questions.question: Your Spring Boot container restarts every 10 minutes with exit code 137 (OOMKilled). Walk through the diagnosis.
questions.title: Diagnosing OOMKilled in Spring Boot Container: Step-by-Step
questions.direct_answer: Exit code 137 = SIGKILL from kernel OOM killer because container exceeded memory limit. Diagnosis order: (1) confirm OOMKilled with `kubectl describe pod` or `docker inspect`; (2) check current heap and non-heap usage with Actuator `/metrics` or `jcmd 1 GC.heap_info`; (3) compare RSS against container limit; (4) take a heap dump with `jmap -dump` and analyze with Eclipse MAT for leaks; (5) fix root cause: tune `MaxRAMPercentage`, find leak, or raise the limit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical incident-response skills for the most common containerized JVM production issue
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reflexively raising the memory limit without finding root cause — hides a memory leak that grows back to the new limit
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish heap leaks from non-heap (Metaspace, direct buffers) leaks, mention NMT (Native Memory Tracking) for non-heap diagnosis, and explain why JVM error logs do NOT appear for OOMKilled (kill is external)

sections.title: Exit Code 137 Means the Kernel Killed You — the JVM Has No Idea What Happened
sections.content:
When a Spring Boot container exits with code 137 and the orchestrator reports `OOMKilled`, the kill came from outside the JVM. The Linux kernel's OOM killer sent SIGKILL to PID 1 because the container's resident set size exceeded the cgroup memory limit. The JVM had no opportunity to react — no `OutOfMemoryError`, no shutdown hooks, no GC dump.

This is fundamentally different from an in-JVM OutOfMemoryError. An in-JVM OOM is a heap exhaustion event the JVM detects and reports; the process can dump heap, log a stack trace, run shutdown hooks. A kernel OOMKill is a hard external termination — the application logs end mid-sentence and the next thing you see is the new container starting.

The diagnostic challenge is that the most useful evidence (heap state, thread state, native memory breakdown) was inside the killed process and is gone. You must instrument the container to capture that evidence **before** the next kill, or use post-mortem evidence (metrics that were exported, heap dump on OOM if configured) to reconstruct what happened.

sections.title: The Diagnosis Decision Tree
sections.content:
The investigation branches based on what the early observations show. Most cases land in either the heap-leak or non-heap-growth path. ```mermaid flowchart TB Start[Pod restart loop
exit 137 OOMKilled] Start --> Confirm{kubectl describe pod
shows OOMKilled?} Confirm -->|No, just exit 1| OutOfScope[Different issue:
app exception, exit\(1\), missing config] Confirm -->|Yes, OOMKilled| Metrics{Have memory
metrics from before kill?} Metrics -->|Prometheus jvm_memory_used| Plot[Plot heap vs non-heap
vs container.memory_usage] Metrics -->|None| Add[Add Actuator + Prom
wait for next kill] Plot --> Q1{Heap growing
over time?} Q1 -->|Yes| Leak[Heap leak suspected] Q1 -->|Stable, but RSS grows| NonHeap[Non-heap leak: Metaspace
or direct buffers] Q1 -->|Both flat, RSS hits limit fast| Sized[Container under-sized
raise limit OR tune MaxRAMPercentage] Leak --> Dump[jmap -dump:live -F 1
analyze with Eclipse MAT] NonHeap --> NMT[Enable NativeMemoryTracking
jcmd 1 VM.native_memory] Dump --> Fix[Fix code: cache eviction
resource leak, listener leak] NMT --> Fix2[Tune MaxMetaspaceSize
or DirectMemorySize] Sized --> Tune[MaxRAMPercentage 60-65%
or raise container limit] style Start fill:#ffcdd2 style Fix fill:#c8e6c9 style Fix2 fill:#c8e6c9 style Tune fill:#c8e6c9 ```

sections.title: Step 1 — Confirm It Is Actually OOMKilled
sections.content:
Before anything else, confirm the kernel killed the container vs the application exited normally with code 137 (rare but possible). Multiple sources of evidence agree if it is real OOMKill.

```bash
kubectl describe pod payment-service-abc123
# Look for:
#   Last State: Terminated
#     Reason: OOMKilled
#     Exit Code: 137
#     Started: ...
#     Finished: ...
```

For Docker:

```bash
docker inspect <container_id> --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}'
# Output: true 137
```

On the node, `dmesg | grep -i 'killed process'` shows the kernel's OOM kill log entry with the RSS that triggered it. If `OOMKilled: false` but exit was 137, the application was killed by some other SIGKILL source (manual kill, liveness probe failure with `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0`, or an explicit `System.exit(137)`).

sections.title: Step 2 — Read the Memory History (Prometheus, Datadog, JFR)
sections.content:
Without metrics from before the kill, you are blind. The first long-term fix is enabling Spring Boot Actuator + Micrometer with a Prometheus or Datadog exporter so future incidents have a data trail.

Assuming metrics are in place, plot these series for the 30 minutes leading to a kill:

- `container_memory_working_set_bytes` (the cgroup-tracked RSS — what the kernel counts)
- `jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"}` (heap usage)
- `jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="nonheap"}` (Metaspace, code cache, etc.)
- `jvm_buffer_memory_used_bytes` (direct + mapped buffers)

The pattern reveals the root cause:

- **Heap rises monotonically over hours → heap leak.** Application keeps adding objects without releasing them. Likely culprits: unbounded cache, listener registration without deregistration, ThreadLocal that escapes thread lifecycle.
- **Heap is sawtooth (rises, GCs, falls) but Metaspace grows monotonically → classloader leak.** Common in apps that hot-reload classes (frameworks, scripting engines, JSP).
- **Heap stable but direct buffers grow → NIO leak.** Common in Netty/gRPC apps that do not release ByteBufs.
- **All JVM metrics flat but `container_memory_working_set_bytes` near limit → container is just under-sized.** Tune `MaxRAMPercentage` down or raise the limit.

sections.title: Step 3 — Heap Leak Path — Take and Analyze a Heap Dump
sections.content:
If heap is the problem, capture a dump while the container is alive (after another restart, before it OOMKills). Two ways:

**Reactive: heap dump on OOM.** Add to JVM flags:

```
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps/heapdump.hprof
```

Mount `/dumps` as a PersistentVolume so the dump survives container restart. Note: this only fires for in-JVM OOM, not for kernel OOMKill — useful for the Metaspace OOM case but not for cgroup-OOMKill.

**Proactive: dump while running.**

```bash
kubectl exec -it pod/payment-service-abc -- jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof
kubectl cp pod/payment-service-abc:/tmp/heap.hprof ./heap.hprof
```

Analyze with Eclipse MAT (Memory Analyzer Tool). Run the **Leak Suspects** report — it identifies the top object retainers. The classic findings:

- A `ConcurrentHashMap` holding hundreds of thousands of entries with no eviction → add Caffeine cache with size/time eviction.
- Listeners registered to a long-lived bean but never deregistered → each request adds a listener; fix with `@PreDestroy` cleanup.
- ThreadLocal storing user context, escaping thread when async work jumps threads → wrap in try-finally with `remove()`.

sections.title: Step 4 — Non-Heap Leak Path — Native Memory Tracking
sections.content:
If heap is stable but RSS keeps growing, the leak is in non-heap. Enable Native Memory Tracking (NMT) to see the breakdown.

```
-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
```

Then inspect:

```bash
kubectl exec -it pod/payment-service-abc -- jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary
```

The output shows committed memory by category: Java Heap, Class (Metaspace), Thread, Code, GC, Internal. The category that grows over time is your leak.

**Metaspace leak.** Common with JSP, Groovy scripting, hot-reload frameworks, or any code that creates classloaders dynamically. Set `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m` to bound it (turns the leak into an in-JVM `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` instead of an OOMKill, giving you a stack trace pointing at the leaky classloader).

**Direct buffer leak.** Common in Netty, gRPC, NIO-heavy apps. Set `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m` to bound it. Use `-Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=PARANOID` to make Netty log unreleased ByteBufs at WARN level. Each warning includes the allocation site — trace back to the missing `release()`.

**Thread leak.** Each thread costs ~1MB of stack. If threads grow unbounded (each request creates a thread without joining), thread stack memory consumes the headroom. Fix the thread pool sizing or find the missing pool.

sections.title: Step 5 — If There Is No Leak, the Container Is Just Too Small
sections.content:
Sometimes the diagnosis is anticlimactic: no leak, just an under-sized container. The application's working set legitimately needs more memory than the limit allows.

Check `MaxRAMPercentage`. If it is 75% in a 512Mi container, the heap gets ~384Mi. Spring Boot's Metaspace alone needs 100–150Mi. Add 50Mi for thread stacks (default 50 Tomcat threads), 50Mi for code cache, 30Mi for GC overhead. That is 230Mi for non-heap, leaving only 128Mi headroom — not enough.

Two fixes:

- **Lower `MaxRAMPercentage` to 60%.** Heap becomes ~307Mi, non-heap headroom becomes ~205Mi. Fewer GCs caused by tighter heap; more headroom for non-heap. Try this first; it is free.
- **Raise the container limit to 1Gi.** Heap becomes ~768Mi, headroom 256Mi. More expensive but appropriate if the app legitimately needs the heap.

Do not blindly double the limit without checking heap pressure. If heap usage was at 90% of `-Xmx` consistently, the heap is undersized and raising helps. If heap usage was at 50%, the issue is non-heap and raising the heap proportion makes it worse.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Long-Term Hardening
sections.content:
**Heap dump on OOM cost.** Writing a 4Gi heap dump to disk takes 30+ seconds and adds disk pressure. In a tight-resource environment, this can cascade. Mitigation: write to a fast local disk or a dedicated PVC, not the container's overlay filesystem.

**Increasing the limit hides leaks.** If the team's first response to OOMKill is always raising the limit, leaks accumulate over months until the limit is 8Gi and still climbing. Always do at least Step 2 (check metrics for monotonic growth) before raising the limit.

**Liveness probe interaction.** A pod that is OOMKilling repeatedly is in `CrashLoopBackOff`. Kubernetes increases the restart delay exponentially (10s, 20s, 40s, ..., max 5min). The pod eventually stabilizes if the OOMKill is rare; if it OOMKills every 10 minutes, capacity is permanently degraded.

**Pod Quality of Service.** Burstable pods (requests < limits for memory) get OOMKilled before Guaranteed pods (requests = limits) when the node is under memory pressure. Set memory requests = limits for any pod that cannot tolerate eviction.

**Multi-container pods.** A sidecar (e.g., Envoy, Datadog agent) shares the pod's memory budget. The OOMKill targets the container that exceeded its own limit, but if any container in the pod OOMKills, the whole pod restarts. Always set explicit limits on every container in the pod.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Exit 137 + `OOMKilled: true` = kernel SIGKILL** — the JVM had no warning; no in-process OOM error to read; you must reconstruct from external metrics or post-mortem dumps
- **Plot RSS vs heap vs Metaspace before raising the limit** — monotonic heap growth = leak; stable heap but growing Metaspace = classloader leak; both flat near limit = under-sized
- **`jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump` works while running** — capture before the next kill rather than relying on `HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` (which does not fire for kernel OOMKill)
- **NMT for non-heap leaks** — `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` then `jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary` shows which category (Class, Thread, Code, Internal) is growing
- **Raising the limit without finding root cause delays the inevitable** — a true leak grows back to whatever limit you set; investigate Step 2 metrics before reaching for `kubectl edit`

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Exit 137 means the kernel killed the container because it exceeded its cgroup memory limit — the JVM had no chance to react.

**Step 1 — confirm OOMKilled, not some other 137 cause**
- `kubectl describe pod` shows `Reason: OOMKilled` and `Exit Code: 137` in the container's last state — confirm both before assuming OOM
- For Docker, `docker inspect <id> --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'` returns true; on the host, `dmesg | grep killed` shows the kernel kill log

**Step 2 — read the memory history before the kill**
- Without metrics from the previous incarnation, you cannot diagnose root cause; if Actuator + Prometheus or Datadog is not in place, install it first and wait for the next kill
- Plot `container_memory_working_set_bytes` (RSS the kernel counts) alongside `jvm_memory_used` (heap) and `jvm_memory_used{area=nonheap}` over the 30 minutes preceding the kill — the shape of the curves tells you the cause

**Step 3 — differentiate heap leak vs non-heap leak vs under-sized container**
- Heap rising monotonically → heap leak; take a heap dump with `jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof`, copy out, analyze with Eclipse MAT's Leak Suspects report — usually finds an unbounded cache, leaked listener, or escaped ThreadLocal
- Heap stable but Metaspace or direct buffers growing → classloader or NIO leak; enable `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` and `jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary` to see which non-heap category is growing
- Both heap and non-heap stable but RSS hits limit fast → the container is just under-sized; tune `MaxRAMPercentage` from 75% down to 60% or raise the limit

**Step 4 — fix the root cause, not the symptom**
- For a heap leak, the fix is in the application code (add eviction, fix the cleanup); for a non-heap leak, the fix may be tuning a JVM flag (`MaxMetaspaceSize`, `MaxDirectMemorySize`) or fixing the leak
- Raising the container limit without finding the leak just delays the next OOMKill until the leak grows into the new limit — leaks have nowhere to go but up

**Long-term hardening**
- Always run with Actuator + Prometheus exporters so the next incident has metrics; add `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` with a PersistentVolume mount so in-JVM OOMs leave a dump behind
- Set memory requests = limits for the QoS Guaranteed class, ensuring the pod is evicted last under node pressure

questions.question: Your CI pipelines started failing with 'toomanyrequests: Rate exceeded' from Docker Hub. How do you fix and prevent this?
questions.title: Docker Hub Rate Limits in CI: Mirror, Cache, and Auth Strategy
questions.direct_answer: Docker Hub limits anonymous pulls to 100 per 6 hours per IP. The fix has three parts: (1) immediate — authenticate CI to a paid Docker Hub account or migrate to a different registry; (2) medium-term — set up a pull-through cache (Harbor, AWS ECR pull-through, Artifactory) so repeated pulls hit the cache instead of Docker Hub; (3) long-term — mirror critical base images to your own registry and pin Dockerfiles to those mirrors. Cache hits cost nothing and avoid the rate limit entirely.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of registry economics, CI scaling, and the dependency on third-party infrastructure
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating it as a 'just authenticate' problem — even authenticated free Docker Hub has 200 pulls/6h, easily blown by a busy CI
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss pull-through caches vs full mirrors, mention ECR public for AWS workloads, and explain how a registry mirror configured at the daemon level transparently redirects all pulls

sections.title: Docker Hub's Rate Limits Are Now a Production Concern, Not a Curiosity
sections.content:
Since Docker introduced rate limiting in 2020, every team running CI/CD at non-trivial scale eventually hits the wall. Anonymous pulls are limited to 100 per 6 hours per IP. Authenticated free accounts get 200. Behind a NAT (everyone in your office or on the same CI runner pool shares one IP), 100 pulls disappear in minutes during a busy build day.

The symptom is sudden CI failure: builds that ran fine yesterday now fail at the FROM line with `toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit`. The fix is not a single switch — it is three layered changes that solve the immediate fire and prevent recurrence.

The root cause is a fragile dependency: every CI build, every node restart, every fresh runner pulls the same handful of base images (`eclipse-temurin`, `nginx`, `postgres`, etc.) directly from Docker Hub. When CI volume scales 10x, Docker Hub bandwidth scales 10x, and you hit the limit. The fix is to **stop hitting Docker Hub directly** and use a cache or mirror in your own infrastructure.

sections.title: Three Pull Topologies
sections.content:
The progression below shows how each fix changes the dependency graph between CI and Docker Hub. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Bad["Anonymous (broken)"] CI1[CI runners] -.100 pulls/6h limit.-> DH1[Docker Hub] end subgraph Auth["Authenticated (better)"] CI2[CI runners] -->|docker login| DH2[Docker Hub
200/6h free
5000/day Pro] end subgraph PT["Pull-through cache (best)"] CI3[CI runners] --> Cache[ECR pull-through
or Harbor proxy] Cache -->|miss only| DH3[Docker Hub] Cache -.cache hits free.-> CI3 end subgraph Mirror["Full mirror (largest scale)"] CI4[CI runners] --> MR[Internal registry
e.g. Artifactory] Periodic[Scheduled sync] --> MR Periodic -->|nightly| DH4[Docker Hub] end style Bad fill:#ffcdd2 style Auth fill:#fff9c4 style PT fill:#c8e6c9 style Mirror fill:#a5d6a7 ``` **Pull-through caches are the sweet spot** for most teams — transparent to Dockerfiles, scales to thousands of pulls per hour, and only fetches from Docker Hub on cache miss.

sections.title: Step 1 — Immediate Fix: Authenticate (10 Minutes)
sections.content:
Buys you 200 pulls/6h instead of 100, and unblocks CI immediately. Not a long-term fix but stops the bleeding.

Create a Docker Hub Pro account (or use your team account). Generate a Personal Access Token (PAT) with read scope. Store it as a CI secret, then login at the start of every job:

```yaml
# GitHub Actions example
- name: Login to Docker Hub
  uses: docker/login-action@v3
  with:
    username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
    password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}
```

Or in Kubernetes, create an `imagePullSecret` and reference it in pod specs. For self-hosted Docker daemons, configure `~/.docker/config.json` with auth.

The limit is per-account when authenticated, not per-IP. So all CI runners using the same account share one 200-pull bucket — still tight for a busy team. A Docker Pro subscription bumps it to 5,000/day; Team and Business tiers go higher. This often costs less than building your own mirror.

sections.title: Step 2 — Medium-Term Fix: Pull-Through Cache (1 Day)
sections.content:
A pull-through cache sits between your CI and Docker Hub. On cache hit (almost always for popular base images), the cache serves the image without contacting Docker Hub. On cache miss, the cache fetches from Docker Hub, stores the image, and serves it. Subsequent pulls of the same image are free.

**AWS ECR pull-through cache.** Create a pull-through cache rule in ECR pointing to Docker Hub. Then in Dockerfiles, replace `FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine` with `FROM <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/docker-hub/eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine`. ECR pulls through Docker Hub on first request, caches forever.

```bash
aws ecr create-pull-through-cache-rule \
  --ecr-repository-prefix docker-hub \
  --upstream-registry-url registry-1.docker.io
```

**Self-hosted Harbor or Artifactory proxy.** Both support "proxy cache" projects that mirror upstream registries. Configure your Docker daemon's `/etc/docker/daemon.json` with `"registry-mirrors": ["https://harbor.internal"]` — then `docker pull eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine` transparently goes through Harbor. No Dockerfile changes needed.

**Containerd's mirror config.** For Kubernetes nodes using containerd, edit `/etc/containerd/config.toml` to add registry mirrors. All pods on the node transparently use the mirror.

```toml
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".registry.mirrors."docker.io"]
  endpoint = ["https://harbor.internal"]
```

sections.title: Step 3 — Long-Term Fix: Vendor Critical Images Into Your Own Registry
sections.content:
For images you depend on for production, do not rely on **any** upstream availability. Mirror them into your own registry on a schedule. This protects against:

- Docker Hub outages (rare but disruptive)
- Upstream image deletion or breaking changes (some maintainers force-push tags)
- Supply-chain attacks (malicious push to upstream)
- Geopolitical disruptions (registries blocked in some regions)

A simple cron-based sync using `skopeo`:

```bash
skopeo sync --src docker --dest docker \
  --src-creds dockerhub-user:$DOCKERHUB_TOKEN \
  --dest-creds ci:$INTERNAL_REGISTRY_TOKEN \
  eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine \
  internal-registry.company.com/mirror/
```

Run nightly via cron or GitHub Actions schedule. Pin Dockerfiles to your internal registry: `FROM internal-registry.company.com/mirror/eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine`. You now control the image lifecycle entirely.

For extra safety, **pin to digests** as well as tags: `FROM internal-registry.company.com/mirror/eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine@sha256:abc123...`. Even a malicious internal-registry push cannot change the digest.

**For Kubernetes**, use a mutating admission webhook (Kyverno) to rewrite all `image:` references that point to docker.io to your internal registry automatically. Developers write `nginx:latest` in deployments; the webhook transforms it to `internal-registry.company.com/mirror/nginx:latest` before the pod is created.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
**Cost of running your own mirror.** Harbor on a small VM is essentially free; ECR pull-through is pennies per GB stored. Compare against Docker Pro/Team subscription costs; for most teams, infrastructure-based caching is cheaper at moderate scale.

**Cache freshness.** A pull-through cache stores images indefinitely by default. If upstream pushes a security fix to `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine`, your cache still serves the old version until you invalidate. Configure cache TTL or run periodic `skopeo sync` to refresh. The trade-off: shorter TTL = more upstream hits; longer TTL = stale images.

**Authentication complexity.** Adding auth to every CI job, every Kubernetes node, every developer workstation, is real toil. Pull-through caches with public read access (Harbor proxy projects can be configured this way) eliminate auth on the read path while keeping push protected.

**Multi-region setups.** If CI runs in multiple regions, a single central cache becomes the bottleneck. Either deploy regional caches (more cost) or use ECR pull-through which is per-region by design.

**ImagePullSecrets in Kubernetes.** Each namespace needs the secret. Use the kubernetes-replicator or sealed-secrets to propagate, or rely on a service mesh to inject auth. Operational overhead is manageable but real.

**Air-gapped environments.** No outbound internet means full vendoring is the only option — all images must be in your internal registry, synced from outside the airgap on a schedule. Skopeo + digital media transfer is the standard pattern.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **100 pulls / 6h anonymous, 200 authenticated** — a busy CI behind one NAT can blow through 100 pulls in minutes; authentication is just a stopgap
- **Pull-through caches are the highest-ROI fix** — transparent (mostly), scales infinitely, only hits Docker Hub on cache miss; ECR / Harbor / Artifactory all support it
- **Configure mirrors at the daemon/containerd level** — no Dockerfile changes needed; `registry-mirrors` in daemon.json or containerd's mirror config redirects pulls transparently
- **Vendor production-critical images into your own registry** — protects against upstream outages, deletions, and supply-chain attacks; pin to digests for reproducibility
- **`skopeo sync` for scheduled mirroring** — simple cron-based mirror is the canonical pattern; pairs well with admission webhooks that rewrite docker.io references in K8s manifests

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Docker Hub rate limits hit every CI eventually — the right fix has three layers depending on how much pain you can tolerate while you fix it.

**Immediate — authenticate**
- Create a Docker Hub account, generate a Personal Access Token, configure CI to `docker login` at the start of every job; the limit goes from 100 per 6 hours to 200 per 6 hours per account
- This buys you a few hours of breathing room, not a real fix; busy CI burns through 200 pulls quickly when many jobs build new images concurrently
- A Docker Pro subscription raises the limit to 5,000/day — often cheaper and simpler than building infrastructure if you are a small team

**Medium-term — pull-through cache**
- A pull-through cache is a registry that sits between your CI and Docker Hub; on the first request for an image, it pulls from Docker Hub and caches; on subsequent requests, it serves from cache without touching Docker Hub
- AWS ECR has built-in pull-through cache rules; Harbor and Artifactory both support proxy-cache projects; all three are zero or near-zero cost at moderate scale
- Configure the Docker daemon's `registry-mirrors` to point at the cache, or for Kubernetes nodes configure containerd's mirror config; pulls become transparent — no Dockerfile changes needed

**Long-term — vendor critical images**
- For images you depend on for production, do not rely on Docker Hub being available; mirror them into your own registry on a nightly schedule using `skopeo sync`
- Pin Dockerfiles to your internal registry and to specific digests, not floating tags; a malicious or accidental upstream change cannot affect your builds
- For Kubernetes, use a mutating admission webhook (Kyverno) to rewrite docker.io image references to your internal registry automatically — developers write `nginx:latest`, the webhook transforms it transparently

**Why this layered approach**
- The immediate fix unblocks CI in 10 minutes; the medium-term fix solves the problem for the next year; the long-term fix protects against the next outage or supply-chain incident
- Each layer is independently valuable; you can stop at any point if the trade-off no longer makes sense for your scale

questions.question: Your container can't reach a service running on the host (postgres, localhost API, etc.). How do you debug and fix it?
questions.title: Container-to-Host Networking: Debugging localhost from Inside a Container
questions.direct_answer: Inside a container, `localhost` refers to the container itself, not the host. To reach host services use `host.docker.internal` (Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows, and Linux with `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway`), or the host's actual LAN IP, or use `--network=host`. In production Kubernetes, host services are exposed via a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service or accessed via the node IP plus `hostNetwork: true` for the client pod.

interviewer_intent.testing: Networking fundamentals — specifically the namespace boundary that confuses every Docker beginner
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hardcoding `localhost:5432` from inside a container expecting it to reach the host's PostgreSQL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain network namespaces, the different behaviors on Linux vs macOS/Windows (Docker Desktop has a VM in between), and the production K8s pattern of running databases as managed services or in StatefulSets

sections.title: `localhost` Inside a Container Is Not Your Host — It's the Container
sections.content:
The most common Docker networking confusion: a developer runs PostgreSQL on their laptop (`localhost:5432`), starts a Spring Boot container with `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb`, and gets `Connection refused`. The container starts fine, the database is running, but the connection fails.

The reason is **network namespaces**. Each container has its own isolated network namespace. Inside that namespace, `localhost` (127.0.0.1) refers to the container itself, not the host. The container's `localhost` interface has no PostgreSQL listening on it because PostgreSQL is in a different namespace — the host's.

The fix depends on what you are actually trying to reach: a host service (PostgreSQL on the laptop), another container (use service name on the same network), or a remote machine (use its actual IP/hostname). Each has a different solution. The host-service case is the most subtle because the answer differs between Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows) and native Linux Docker.

sections.title: Network Namespaces and Where `localhost` Points
sections.content:
Each box below has its own loopback interface. They are not the same loopback. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Host["Host machine network namespace"] HL[host: 127.0.0.1] HE[host: eth0 = 192.168.1.42] HSVC[PostgreSQL listening
on 127.0.0.1:5432] HL --- HSVC end subgraph C1["Container 1 namespace"] C1L[container1: 127.0.0.1] C1V[container1: eth0 = 172.17.0.2] C1A[Spring Boot app
tries localhost:5432] C1L --- C1A end HE -.bridge: docker0.-> C1V C1A -.tries 127.0.0.1:5432
FAIL: nothing here.-> C1L C1A -.host.docker.internal:5432
OR 192.168.1.42:5432
WORKS.-> HSVC style Host fill:#fff3e0 style C1 fill:#e3f2fd style HSVC fill:#c8e6c9 ``` The container's `localhost` and the host's `localhost` are **different interfaces in different namespaces** — same name, different routing tables.

sections.title: Diagnosis — Confirm the Right Endpoint Is Reachable
sections.content:
Before changing config, verify what the container can actually reach. Exec into the container and test:

```bash
docker exec -it my-app sh
# Inside the container:

# 1. localhost — will fail for host services
nc -zv localhost 5432
# Expected: connection refused

# 2. host.docker.internal (Docker Desktop, or Linux with --add-host)
nc -zv host.docker.internal 5432
# Expected: succeeded if PostgreSQL listens on the host's all-interfaces or LAN IP

# 3. Host's LAN IP
nc -zv 192.168.1.42 5432
# Expected: succeeded if PostgreSQL allows connections from the bridge subnet

# 4. DNS resolution sanity
nslookup host.docker.internal
# Should resolve to host gateway IP
```

**If `host.docker.internal` does not resolve** on Linux, you need to add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway` to the `docker run` command (or the equivalent in Compose).

**If the LAN IP fails**, PostgreSQL is bound only to `127.0.0.1` on the host. Edit `postgresql.conf` and set `listen_addresses = '*'` (or specifically the bridge subnet), then update `pg_hba.conf` to allow connections from `172.17.0.0/16`. Restart PostgreSQL.

sections.title: Fix — Three Patterns for Three Environments
sections.content:
**Pattern 1: Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows).** `host.docker.internal` works out of the box. Use it everywhere:

```yaml
environment:
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://host.docker.internal:5432/mydb
```

**Pattern 2: Native Linux Docker.** Add the host-gateway alias:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: my-spring-app
    extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://host.docker.internal:5432/mydb
```

Or use the host's LAN IP directly: `jdbc:postgresql://192.168.1.42:5432/mydb`. Less portable across machines but explicit.

**Pattern 3: Best practice — put both in containers.** The reason developers reach for host networking is usually that PostgreSQL is on the host while the app is in a container. The cleaner pattern is to put PostgreSQL in a container too, on the same Compose network:

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
  app:
    image: my-spring-app
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/mydb
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
```

Now `postgres` resolves via Compose's bridge network DNS — no host networking gymnastics needed. This is also the production-shaped setup.

sections.title: Production K8s — You Almost Never Reach the Node
sections.content:
In production Kubernetes, the question changes. Pods rarely reach services on the node directly because:

- Pods can be rescheduled to any node; tying them to a specific host service breaks portability.
- Node services are usually system daemons (kubelet, container runtime), not application services.
- Application services run as pods, and pod-to-pod communication uses Service DNS.

The correct production patterns:

**For a pod-to-pod service.** Create a Kubernetes Service. Pods reach it by `<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` or just `<service-name>` in the same namespace.

**For a managed external service (RDS, Cloud SQL).** Create a `Service` of type `ExternalName` that maps an internal DNS name to the external endpoint:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: prod-db.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
```

Apps connect to `postgres:5432` regardless of environment — dev points to a Pod, prod points to RDS via ExternalName.

**For a node-level service** (rare — e.g., a daemon running on each node). Use `hostNetwork: true` in the Pod spec so the pod shares the node's network namespace. Then `localhost` inside the pod refers to the node. Used carefully — it sacrifices Pod isolation.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Common Pitfalls
sections.content:
**`--network=host` is the sledgehammer.** Removes the network namespace entirely. The container shares the host's network stack. Now `localhost:5432` works — but you also lose port-isolation (two containers cannot both bind 8080), and the container can reach every other localhost service the host runs. Sometimes appropriate for development, almost never for production.

**Bind-address mistakes.** A common variant: PostgreSQL is configured to listen only on `127.0.0.1`. Even with correct host networking, the container still cannot connect because PostgreSQL refuses bridge-network IPs. Fix by editing `postgresql.conf` and `pg_hba.conf` to accept the bridge subnet, OR bind PostgreSQL to `0.0.0.0` (less secure if the host is exposed).

**Firewall and SELinux.** On RHEL/CentOS hosts, firewalld blocks bridge-to-host traffic by default. Either add the bridge interface to a trusted zone or disable firewalld for development. SELinux can also block the connection — check `getenforce` and audit logs.

**Docker Desktop's VM hop.** On macOS and Windows, Docker runs inside a Linux VM. `host.docker.internal` works because Docker Desktop installs a special networking stack that bridges through the VM. Performance is slightly worse than native Linux containers but invisible for most workloads.

**Kubernetes vs Docker behavior.** `host.docker.internal` does not exist in vanilla Kubernetes. The conceptual equivalent is `Service` with `ExternalName` or `hostNetwork: true`. Migrating local Compose setups to K8s requires rewriting these connection patterns.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`localhost` in a container is the container, not the host** — each network namespace has its own loopback; this is the foundational insight everyone learns the hard way
- **`host.docker.internal` is the canonical answer** — works on Docker Desktop natively; on Linux add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway`
- **Better fix: containerize the dependency too** — PostgreSQL in a Compose service alongside the app eliminates the host-network problem entirely and matches production shape
- **`--network=host` removes namespace isolation** — makes `localhost` work but sacrifices port isolation; appropriate for some dev cases, rarely for prod
- **Production K8s uses Services, not host networking** — `ExternalName` Services map app-friendly DNS names to RDS/Cloud SQL endpoints; `hostNetwork: true` is reserved for daemon-style pods that genuinely need node access

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Inside a container, `localhost` refers to the container itself, not the host machine — that is the entire reason connections to host services fail.

**Why localhost fails**
- Each container runs in its own network namespace with its own loopback interface; the host's loopback (where PostgreSQL is listening) is in a different namespace and not reachable as `127.0.0.1` from inside the container
- This catches every developer once — same hostname, completely different network

**Three fixes from worst to best**
- `host.docker.internal:5432` — a Docker-provided DNS name that resolves to the host gateway; works out of the box on Docker Desktop, requires `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway` on native Linux Docker; the most portable Docker-only fix
- The host's actual LAN IP — `192.168.1.42:5432` — always works if PostgreSQL is configured to listen on that interface and `pg_hba.conf` allows connections from the bridge subnet; more explicit but tied to a specific host
- Containerize the dependency — add a `postgres` service to your `docker-compose.yml` so the database lives in the same Compose network; the app reaches `postgres:5432` via service-name DNS; no host-networking complexity at all and matches production shape

**Important diagnostic steps**
- `docker exec -it <container> nc -zv host.docker.internal 5432` confirms whether the container can reach the host service; if this fails, the issue is on the host side (PostgreSQL bound only to localhost, firewall blocking the bridge subnet)
- Check PostgreSQL's `listen_addresses` in `postgresql.conf` — if it is the default `localhost`, change to `*` or the bridge subnet; also add an entry to `pg_hba.conf` for `172.17.0.0/16` (the docker0 bridge subnet)

**Kubernetes is different**
- In K8s, pods almost never reach services on the node directly — they reach other pods via Kubernetes Services or external services via `ExternalName` Services that map internal DNS names to RDS/Cloud SQL endpoints
- For the rare pod that genuinely needs node access (Datadog agent, log collector), `hostNetwork: true` shares the node's network namespace and makes `localhost` mean the node — used sparingly because it sacrifices Pod isolation
